lesson_title: Count a Trillion Trillion Molecules With a Kitchen Scale
hook_text: You can count particles too small to see — with the same trick your grandmother uses for eggs.
clip_script: Chemists face a counting problem: atoms are too small to count, yet reactions happen atom by atom. The fix is a trick every kitchen already uses — count by weighing. If one egg weighs 50 grams, then 600 grams of eggs is 12 eggs. Nobody counted; the scale did. The mole is the chemist's dozen, scaled up absurdly: 6,02 times 10 to the 23 particles. The periodic table is the price list — it quotes what one mole of each element weighs. One mole of carbon dioxide weighs 44 grams. So put 22 grams of the gas on a scale, and you KNOW, without counting, that you hold half a mole: hundreds of billions of trillions of molecules, tallied by grocery-store equipment.
visual_style: Kitchen scale piled with eggs morphing into a beaker of gas molecules; periodic table flickering like a supermarket price board; giant counter spinning to 6,02 × 10²³.
mood: Kitchen-hack cleverness scaled to cosmic numbers.
pacing: Homely egg-counting open, quick price-list beat, number-explosion reveal, tidy exam-hook close.
